Every one of those conditions must be met at once: the rider has fully stopped, the red has lasted unreasonably long or the signal is not detecting the bicycle, and nobody approaching is close enough to be an immediate hazard. narration.text: Motorcyclists must obey the same traffic laws as other drivers, but their smaller size and lack of protection call for extra care from everyone around them. In this unit you will learn why motorcycles are hard to judge, how much following distance and merging room to give them, what to do when one passes you, why crowding a motorcycle is illegal, and the rules for lane sharing, lane splitting and lane filtering. You will also see the most common motorcycle-car crash and how right-of-way laws protect riders. Several numbers appear, so the unit compares them directly.

Because motorcycles are small, their speed and distance are hard to judge as they approach. Leave at least as much following distance behind a motorcycle as behind any other vehicle, since a rider may have trouble controlling it and weave. When moving into a lane ahead of a motorcycle, leave as much room behind your vehicle as you would for a car. Motorcycles do not protect riders in a crash the way other vehicles protect their occupants, so these spacing rules matter. Treat a motorcycle as a full vehicle that needs full space, not a smaller one that needs less.

lines.text: Hold lane and speed when passed
Never drive beside one in its lane

narration.text: If a motorcyclist passes you, keep your lane position and speed and let the rider finish the pass. Crowding a motorcyclist is illegal, and you must never drive beside a motorcycle in the same lane. At the same time, a motorcyclist may legally share your lane to pass you in slow or stopped traffic, and you must not block or try to stop them. So the rule runs one way: a rider may share your lane in those conditions, but you may not move into a motorcycle's lane beside it. Hold steady and let the rider move through safely.

Lane splitting is legal only where two or more lanes run in the same direction with traffic moving, at no more than twenty-five mph and no more than fifteen mph faster than the surrounding traffic. Lane filtering lets a motorcycle move between stopped vehicles, such as at a light or in a jam, where two or more lanes run the same way, at no more than fifteen mph above the traffic speed. Both need two or more lanes going the same way. The difference is whether traffic is moving or stopped, and that difference decides which limits apply.

These two terms are easy to swap. Lane splitting happens in moving traffic and carries two limits, twenty-five mph and fifteen mph over traffic, while lane filtering happens in stopped traffic and carries only the fifteen mph over traffic limit. If a question describes a motorcycle passing between moving cars at thirty mph, it is outside the splitting limit. If it describes a motorcycle moving between cars stopped at a light, that is filtering, and the only limit is fifteen over the traffic speed. Sort by moving or stopped first, then apply the matching limits.

The most common motorcycle-car crashes happen at urban intersections, many when a driver fails to yield and turns left across an oncoming motorcycle's path. That pattern ties back to the first rule in this unit: because motorcycles are small, their speed and distance are hard to judge. Right-of-way laws protect motorcyclists like everyone else, and motorcyclists may use high-occupancy vehicle lanes. Before you turn left, look for oncoming motorcycles as carefully as for cars, and yield to them exactly as you would to any other vehicle.

Splitting is for moving traffic at up to twenty-five mph and fifteen over, filtering for stopped traffic at fifteen over. title.text: Trucks and buses on the road

narration.text: Commercial vehicles share the highway with you every day, and their size changes how you should drive around them. This unit defines a commercial vehicle and then covers how to pass one safely: checking clearance, allowing extra time, knowing when not to pass, using hills to your advantage, and finishing the pass. It also covers what to do when a truck passes you, how to meet one head-on, why trucks often look slower than they are, and why patience works better than honking. The next unit then covers following and turning near trucks.

A commercial vehicle is a motor vehicle or combination weighing over twenty-six thousand pounds that carries passengers or property, and every bus of any size, school buses included, counts too, as do smaller vehicles displaying hazardous materials placards. So a vehicle can be commercial because of its weight, because it is a bus, or because it carries hazardous materials. Trucks and buses run under operating restrictions and may use speed limiters, and honking, aggressive driving or weaving around them only adds dangerous distractions. Patience is part of sharing the road with them.

Before passing a commercial vehicle, make sure you have safe clearance beside, behind and ahead of your vehicle. Passing a commercial vehicle on a level highway takes three to five seconds longer than passing a car, and you still must be back in your lane before coming within one hundred feet of oncoming traffic. If you will exit or turn off soon, stay behind the commercial vehicle instead of passing it. Those extra seconds and that return distance add up, so only start a pass when you have the clearance and the time to finish it.

lines.text: Uphill: trucks slow, easier to pass

narration.text: Here is the trap. Commercial vehicles slow down going uphill, making them easier to pass, but speed up going downhill, so allow more distance for a downhill pass. Some drivers assume a truck is always slow and try to pass it on a downgrade, only to find the truck gaining speed beside them. Finish a pass of a commercial vehicle quickly, return to your lane only once its front shows in your rearview mirror, and keep your speed afterward. Uphill makes passing easier, downhill makes it harder, and the mirror check tells you when you are clear.

narration.text: While a truck or bus is passing you, move to the far side of your lane, ease off slightly, and never speed up. When meeting a commercial vehicle head-on, keep as far right as you can; the wind turbulence pushes the two vehicles apart, not together. Large commercial vehicles often seem slower than they really are, and many car-truck crashes at intersections come from misjudging their speed and distance. So give passing trucks room, keep right when meeting them, and assume a large vehicle is moving faster than it looks before you cross or turn in front of it.

narration.text: This unit continues the truck lessons with the situations where most car-truck trouble begins: cutting in front, following behind, and turning. You will learn why a car and a loaded tractor-trailer stop over very different distances, how far back to stay so the driver can see you, what to do with your headlights at night, how to treat a merging truck and a truck stopped on a hill, why trucks swing wide on right turns, and where a truck driver's no zones are. The numbers in this unit are large and memorable, so they are worth learning exactly.

lines.text: Car at fifty-five: one hundred thirty to forty feet
Loaded truck: over four hundred feet

narration.text: Cutting in close ahead of a bus or truck is especially dangerous, because you are likely in its blind spot and it cannot slow quickly enough to avoid you. At fifty-five mph an average car can stop within one hundred thirty to one hundred forty feet, while a fully loaded tractor-trailer may need more than four hundred feet. Put those two together and the danger is clear: a truck driver who cannot see you, in a vehicle that needs far more distance to stop, cannot react if you brake just ahead. Leave plenty of room before moving in front of a truck.

lines.text: Stay visible in its side mirrors

narration.text: Following a truck too closely blocks your view of the road ahead, so stay far enough back that the driver can see you in the side mirrors. Keeping a safe distance behind a commercial vehicle also gives you time to react if it stops suddenly. Always dim your headlights when following a commercial vehicle at night, because its large side mirrors reflect light into the driver's eyes. When a commercial vehicle is merging, it needs more time than a car to reach normal speed, so be ready to slow down or change lanes and give it the time it needs.

lines.text: Sit on the left side of your lane
Driver sees you in the mirror

narration.text: Stopped behind a commercial vehicle on an upgrade, leave room for it to roll back slightly as it starts, and sit on the left side of your lane where the driver can see you. The truck may roll back slightly as it starts, so the gap behind it protects your car. Positioning to the left of your lane puts your vehicle in view of the truck's side mirror, so the driver knows you are there. Room plus visibility is the pattern for every situation around a truck. Leave room for the rollback, sit on the left side of your lane, and make sure the driver can see you in the side mirror.

Many commercial vehicles swing wide for right turns, so never pass one on the right when it might be turning right. In a turn, a vehicle's back wheels track inside the path of its front wheels, and that gap grows with the length of the vehicle. A turning truck may leave an open space on its right just before turning, so watch its turn signals closely. That open space is not an invitation to pass: many commercial vehicles swing wide for right turns, so never pass one on the right when it might turn right. Watch the turn signals of every commercial vehicle closely.

Up to two hundred feet behind

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think a truck's blind spot is only beside the cab. A truck's no zones are blind spots where the driver may not see up to twenty feet ahead of the cab, along either side of the trailer, or up to two hundred feet behind. So the rear no zone is ten times longer than the front one. A car following closely, even well behind the cab, can be invisible. If you cannot see the truck's side mirrors, assume the driver cannot see you, and either drop back or move ahead to a spot where you are visible.

So you leave a gap and move to the left part of your lane. That combines the two ideas behind every truck rule in this unit: give the truck room, and stay where its driver can see you in the mirror. Room and visibility are what keep you safe.

narration.text: To wrap up, never cut in close ahead of a truck or bus: you are likely in its blind spot, and a loaded tractor-trailer may need over four hundred feet to stop at fifty-five, compared with one hundred thirty to one hundred forty feet for a car. Follow far enough back to be seen in its side mirrors, dim your headlights at night, and give merging trucks time. On an upgrade, leave rollback room and sit to the left. Trucks swing wide on right turns, so never pass them on the right, and stay out of the no zones: twenty feet ahead, the sides, and two hundred feet behind.

narration.text: Because of a train's size and weight, most collisions between vehicles and trains kill the driver. This unit covers how to recognize a crossing ahead, where to stop when signals are active, when you may start across, which vehicles must stop at every crossing, the danger of a second train, what to do in heavy traffic, the gear-shifting rule, how motorcyclists should cross, how to treat a flag person, and the blue Emergency Notification System sign that lets you report a problem. Two ten-foot rules sit at the center of the unit, and they are easy to confuse.

lines.text: At least ten feet from the rail

narration.text: Warning signs and pavement markings tell you a railroad crossing is ahead, and signs near the track show how many tracks there are. When crossing lights flash, bells ring or gates are down, do not cross, and stop at least ten feet from the nearest rail or gate. Passenger vans, buses and larger trucks must stop at every railroad track even with no train present, and passing any vehicle within one hundred feet of a railroad crossing is illegal. So expect the vehicles ahead to stop at crossings, and never try to pass them there.

lines.text: Stop ten feet before the nearest rail

narration.text: Here is the trap. At a crossing the first ten-foot rule is where you stop, short of the nearest rail or gate, and the second is where you must be able to clear, beyond the far rail, before you start across. Cross the tracks only when traffic ahead has moved and you can clear them without having to stop within ten feet beyond the rails. The two rules use the same number but sit on opposite sides of the tracks. Stop ten feet before when signals are active, and never start across unless you can end up at least ten feet past.

lines.text: Heavy traffic: wait behind the tracks

narration.text: After the last car of a train passes, wait until you are sure no second train is coming on another track, and look both ways at every crossing. When traffic is heavy on both sides of a crossing, wait behind the tracks until you can get all the way across, and never race a train. Trains cannot stop as quickly as cars, and their speed and distance are hard to judge, especially at night, so if you hesitate with a train in sight, stop and let it pass. Waiting costs a minute, while misjudging a train can cost your life.

lines.text: Flag person equals a warning device

narration.text: Never shift gears while crossing the tracks; in a manual transmission vehicle, shift down before you enter the crossing. Motorcyclists should approach railroad crossings with caution and should not swerve for a better crossing angle, which can put them into oncoming traffic. Treat a flag person at a railroad crossing the same way you would treat a warning device, and never stop on the tracks. Each of these rules keeps you moving smoothly across the rails or keeps you off them entirely, which is exactly where you want to be when a train might be coming.

lines.text: Dispatchers can stop or slow trains

narration.text: Every highway-rail crossing has a blue Emergency Notification System sign on the crossing posts or control box, with a round-the-clock number for reporting an obstruction or problem that requires stopping trains. Giving the number on the blue ENS sign lets dispatchers pinpoint the crossing and tell trains headed that way to stop or slow down. So if a vehicle stalls on the tracks, or you see something blocking a crossing, the sign gives you a direct way to warn the railroad. Note where the sign is the next time you pass a crossing, so you can find it in an emergency.

Passenger vans, buses and larger trucks must stop at every railroad track even with no train present, and passing any vehicle within one hundred feet of a railroad crossing is illegal. So the answer is passenger vans, buses and larger trucks. When you follow one of them toward a crossing, expect it to stop, leave room behind it, and never try to pass it within one hundred feet of the tracks, even if the crossing looks clear.

With lights, bells or gates active, stop at least ten feet from the nearest rail, and cross only when you can clear ten feet beyond the rails. Vans, buses and larger trucks stop at every track, and no one may pass within one hundred feet of a crossing. Watch for a second train, wait behind the tracks in heavy traffic, never race a train, never shift on the tracks, obey flag persons, and use the blue ENS sign to report problems.

rationale.text: Where a work zone has no reduced limit posted, the ordinary posted limit still applies.

narration.text: Highway work zones are areas where road construction or maintenance is under way, and the rules there protect both the workers and you. This unit explains the penalties for disobeying a flag person or the speed limit, the extra fine for speeding, which limit applies when no reduced limit is posted, how to plan for delays, and how to keep your distance from crews and equipment. It then turns to the zipper merge, the method Minnesota recommends when a lane closes and traffic backs up, and explains why it works better than the early merge many drivers were taught.

lines.text: Disobeying a flagger or limit: penalty
No reduced limit: usual limit applies

narration.text: In a work zone, disobeying a flag person or the speed limit brings a violation and a financial penalty. Speeding in a work zone adds a three hundred dollar fine on top of the regular speeding ticket. Where a work zone has no reduced speed limit posted, the ordinary posted limit still applies. So there is no situation in which a work zone has no limit at all. Either a reduced limit is posted and you obey it, or the ordinary posted limit remains in force, and in both cases speeding carries the extra three hundred dollar fine.

lines.text: Machinery may work at any hour

narration.text: Work zones may have machinery moving or parked at any hour, so be patient, expect delays at peak times and follow the signs and markings workers set up. Stay alert in a work zone and shift your lane position to keep away from workers and equipment, because lanes may be changed and distractions can be fatal. In other words, plan extra time, put the phone away, and watch the new lane layout rather than the old lines. Giving workers and equipment as much space as your lane allows is the simplest way to keep everyone in the zone safe.

lines.text: Lane closed ahead and traffic backs up
Stay in your lane to the merge point

narration.text: In a zipper merge, once a lane closed ahead sign appears and traffic backs up, stay in your lane to the merge point and then take turns merging into the open lane. When traffic is heavy and slow, staying in your current lane until the point where drivers can take turns is the safer choice. Both lanes stay full right up to the merge point, and then drivers alternate, one from each lane. Everyone moves through the closure in turn, and no one has to force their way in at the last moment. Stay in your lane, reach the merge point, and take your turn.

lines.text: Longer backups, more crashes, more rage

narration.text: Here is the trap. Drivers have traditionally been taught to merge early, but early merging leads to longer backups, more crashes and more road rage. It can feel courteous to move over as soon as you see the lane closed sign, but when traffic is heavy and slow, that habit leaves one lane jammed and the other empty. Staying in your current lane until the point where drivers can take turns is the safer choice. When a question asks for the recommended way to merge into a lane closure in heavy traffic, the zipper merge is the answer, not the early merge.

lines.text: Backups up to forty percent shorter
Safer for workers, narrower speed gaps

narration.text: The zipper merge can shorten traffic backups by up to forty percent. Zipper merging also improves worker safety in lane closures, narrows the speed gap between lanes, eases congestion at freeway interchanges, feels fairer and cuts road rage. Those benefits all come from using both lanes fully and taking turns at one point. Because every driver moves forward together, no lane sits idle, lane changes become easier, and nobody feels cut off. And because worker safety improves in lane closures, the zipper merge helps the crews as well as the drivers.

Here is a quick check: you enter a work zone where no reduced speed limit is posted. What speed limit applies? Recall the rule. Where a work zone has no reduced speed limit posted, the ordinary posted limit still applies. And speeding in a work zone adds a three hundred dollar fine on top of the regular speeding ticket, while disobeying a flag person or the speed limit brings a violation and a financial penalty. So the answer is the ordinary posted limit, and exceeding it in the zone still brings the extra fine. There is no zone without a limit.

lines.text: Zipper merge at the merge point

narration.text: To sum up, in a work zone disobeying a flag person or the speed limit brings a violation and a financial penalty, speeding adds a three hundred dollar fine, and where no reduced limit is posted the ordinary limit applies. Machinery may work at any hour, so be patient, expect delays and shift your lane position away from workers. When a lane closes and traffic backs up, use the zipper merge: stay in your lane to the merge point and take turns. Early merging lengthens backups, while the zipper merge can shorten them by up to forty percent and makes the closure safer and fairer.
